overview.body:
**Pállas** ​(*pallas*) — ‌Titan of ‌warcraft · ​celestial bronze ​spear ​· father ​of Nike/Kratos/Bia/Zelos ​— belongs ‌to the ​Greek ​tradition, where ‌it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Warcraft, ‌Strategy, Celestial ​Bronze". The ​name means ​"Titan of ​warcraft; ​father of ‌Nike, Kratos, ​Bia, and ‌Zelos"[^1].

​**Pállas** is ‌the Titan ​who embodies ‌the craft ​of ‌war itself ​— not ​mere berserk ‌rage but ‌the ‌disciplined art ​of spear, ​shield, and ‌strategy. He ​is ​the father ‌of Nike ​(Victory), Kratos ​(Strength), Bia ‌(Force), ​and Zelos ‌(Rivalry): war ​produces its ​own children, ​and ​they never ‌leave his ‌household.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ‌name ​as **Pállas** ​and serves ‌its temple ‌at [pállas.com](https://xn--pllas-xqa.com). ‌The ‌original carries ​both stress ‌and vowel ​length, and ​exactly ​one historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which ​places the ‌name in ​Tier 1. ​The plain ​ASCII ‌form *pallas* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Greek ​as ​**Πάλλας**. Etymologically ​it means ​"Titan ​of warcraft; ‌father ​of Nike, ​Kratos, ‌Bia, and ​Zelos"[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ‌*pallas* survives ​only because ​the ​early domain-name ​system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; it ‌is ​a technological ‌compromise, ​not an ‌ancient spelling. ​The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Pállas** ​recovers the ‌stress ‌accent of ‌the ​original directly ​in ‌the address ​bar. The ​original ‌carries both ​stress ​and vowel ‌length, ​and exactly ‌one ​historically valid ​Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which places ‌the ‌name in ​Tier ‌1.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- ‌**p** → ‌**P** ‌— Pi, ​capitalized
- ‌**a** ​→ **á** ​— ​Acute on ‌alpha
​- **l** ​→ ​**l** — ‌Lambda
​- **l** ​→ **l** ​— ‌Lambda
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ‌Alpha
- ​**s** ‌→ **s** ‌— ​Sigma

The ​canonical temple ​for ​this name ‌is ‌served at ​**pállas.com**[^2].

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/ˈpal.las/** ​— ​Attic ‌Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

​- ‌**Pál-** ​— Voiceless ‌labial ​stop ​plus ​alpha ​with ​acute: the ‌stressed ​syllable ‌rises ​in ‌pitch.
- ​**-las** ‌— ​Lambda-alpha-sigma, ‌a ​clear, ​martial close.

‌For ‌the ‌modern ​speaker, ​the ‌closest approximation ​is: ​'PAHL-lahs' ‌— ​the ​first ‌syllable carries ​the ‌ancient ​Greek ​pitch ​accent.

​Kindred and ‌historical ‌forms ​of ‌the ​name:

​- **Greek** ‌— ‌Πάλλας ‌(Pállas), ‌the ​Titan ‌of warcraft

​Pállas ​is ​a ‌short, ​sharp name ​whose ​acute ‌on ​the ​first ​syllable gives ‌it ​a ‌commander's ​ring. ‌The ​meaning is ‌uncertain; ‌ancient ​sources ​connect ​it ​with 'brandish' ‌(πάλλω) ‌or ​'spear'.

domains.body:
**Pállas** ​is ‌the ‌Titan who ​embodies ​the ​craft ​of ​war itself ‌— ​not ​mere ‌berserk ​rage ‌but the ​disciplined ‌art ​of ​spear, ​shield, and ​strategy. ​He ‌is ​the ‌father ​of Nike ‌(Victory), ​Kratos ‌(Strength), ​Bia ‌(Force), and ​Zelos ​(Rivalry): ‌war ‌produces ‌its ​own children, ​and ‌they ​never ​leave ‌his household.[^1]

​### ​The ‌Spear

​His ‌signature ​weapon, cast ​in ​celestial ​bronze, ‌the ‌metal of ​the ‌gods.

​### ​Strategy

‌War ‌as calculation: ‌the ‌arrangement ​of ‌forces ​before the ​clash.

​### ‌Father ​of ​Personifications

​Nike, Kratos, ‌Bia, ​and ​Zelos ​are ‌born from ​his ‌lineage.

​### ‌Celestial ​Bronze

‌The divine ‌alloy ​that ​marks ​the ​armament of ‌gods ‌and ​Titans.

sources.citation: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca.
Hesiod, Theogony, Loeb Classical Library No. 57, 700 BCE.

mythology.body:
Pállas ​belongs to ‌the older ‌generation of ​gods, ​the Titans. ​His myth ​is less ​narrative ‌than genealogical ​and thematic: ​he is ‌the source ​from ‌which the ​personifications of ‌war's consequences ​descend.[^1]

​### Son ​of Kreios ​and Eurybia ​(Genealogy)

‌Hesiod names ​Pállas as ‌the son ​of ‌the Titan ​Kreios (Crius) ‌and the ​sea-power ‌Eurybia. From ​this union ​of sky-lineage ‌and maritime ‌force ‌comes a ​deity whose ​domain is ‌the ​practical mastery ​of conflict.[^2]

‌### The ​Children ​of Pállas ‌(Children)

By ​the Oceanid ‌Styx, ​Pállas fathers ​Nike (Victory), ​Kratos (Strength), ​Bia ‌(Force), and ‌Zelos (Rivalry). ​These are ‌not ​companions chosen ​at random; ‌they are ‌the necessary ‌entourage ‌of any ​war. Where ‌Pállas is, ​they ​follow.

### ​War in ‌Heaven (Titanomachy)

​As ​a Titan, ​Pállas belongs ‌to the ​older ​order overthrown ​by Zeus ‌and the ​Olympians. ‌His children, ​however, side ‌with Zeus ​— a ‌sign ‌that the ​forces of ​warcraft can ​be ​transferred from ‌one regime ‌to the ​next.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Pállas ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Greek ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section[^1].

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Πάλλας, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​warcraft ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(spear ​and ​shield). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

meditation.body:
Pállas ​is ‌war ‌as a ​technology. ​He ​is ​not ​the bloodlust ‌of ​Árēs ​nor ‌the ​strategic ‌wisdom of ​Athēnâ; ‌he ​is ​the ​craft itself ​— ​the ‌forging ​of ‌weapons, ​the drilling ‌of ​formations, ‌the ​transmission ‌of technique ​from ​one ‌generation ‌of ‌fighters ​to the ​next. ‌His ​children ​are ‌not emotions ​but ​outcomes: ‌victory, ​strength, ‌force, ​rivalry.

To ​think ​about ​Pállas ‌is ‌to ask ​whether ‌war ​can ​ever ‌be ‌pure craft, ‌divorced ‌from ​the ‌reasons ​for which ​it ​is ‌fought. ​The ​Greeks ​suspected not; ‌even ​a ​craftsman ​of ‌battle must ​eventually ‌choose ​a ‌side. ​His ‌children followed ‌Zeus, ​and ​so, ​in ​the end, ‌did ‌the ​craft.[^1]
